records.name: Apollo 11 Lunar Surface Television Camera
records.short_description: The Apollo 11 black-and-white lunar television camera transmitted live surface views. NASA sources place its tripod approximately 30 ft or 40 ft from the Lunar Module, so the exact reported distance is unresolved. It was left on the Moon; its present physical condition is unknown.

carousel_image.alt: Apollo 11 astronaut Edwin Aldrin unloads the EASEP beside the Lunar Module; the lunar surface television camera is visible beyond the Lunar Module's right leg.
carousel_image.image_note: Wide-context archival photograph. The NASA NSSDC catalog specifically identifies the distant object beyond the Lunar Module's right leg as the lunar surface TV camera; it is not a close-up of the camera.

details.overview: The Apollo 11 Lunar Surface Television Camera was the black-and-white surface camera used to transmit live television views of the first crewed lunar landing and surface activities to Earth.
details.primary_purpose: To provide television coverage of the astronauts’ first steps and subsequent lunar surface activity.
details.mission_role: It supplied the live surface television feed from the Apollo 11 Lunar Module landing site.

its_story.development: NASA’s Apollo 11 Press Kit identifies the camera as a Westinghouse-built black-and-white lunar television camera.
its_story.preparation: It was stowed in the Modularized Equipment Stowage Assembly (MESA) in the Lunar Module descent stage.
its_story.journey: It travelled to the lunar surface aboard the Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle.
its_story.deployment: Deployment of the MESA lowered the camera beside the Lunar Module ladder. Armstrong subsequently mounted it on a tripod. NASA's Press Kit diagram labels the tripod position approximately 30 ft from the LM, whereas the Mission Report prose gives approximately 40 ft; the discrepancy is unresolved.
its_story.final_chapter: NASA archival material shows the camera left on the lunar surface near the Lunar Module. Its later physical condition is not established by the sources reviewed. A separate NASA article on astronaut still photography states that the Hasselblad 500EL Data Camera and lens were left at Tranquility Base. That statement concerns the still-photography camera, not this Westinghouse surface television camera, and is not used as evidence for this record’s ABANDONED status.

why_is_it_there.scientific_engineering_need: The camera provided a live visual record of surface activity to mission controllers and viewers on Earth.
why_is_it_there.mission_requirement: Apollo 11 required television coverage of the first human steps on the Moon and subsequent crew activity.
why_is_it_there.expected_purpose: Transmit a real-time black-and-white television picture from the lunar surface.
why_is_it_there.historical_context: It formed part of the surface communications and documentation system for the first crewed lunar landing.

how_was_it_built.design_and_construction: The camera was manufactured by Westinghouse Electric Corporation. NASA documentation describes a bayonet lens mount and two lenses for different lunar viewing conditions.
how_was_it_built.engineering_approach: A compact, crew-deployable television camera was stowed in the MESA and could be moved to a tripod for a wider view of the work area.
how_was_it_built.how_it_worked: The camera used a 24–32 V DC supply and transmitted black-and-white images at 10 frames per second, with 320 lines per frame.
how_was_it_built.dimensions: Camera body: approximately 0.269 m × 0.165 m × 0.086 m (converted from 10.6 × 6.5 × 3.4 in).
how_was_it_built.power_source: 24–32 V DC electrical supply; the reviewed press kit does not specify the detailed internal power-routing arrangement.
how_was_it_built.mobility_system: Initially attached to the MESA for deployment; later mounted on a tripod by the crew.

records.name: ALSEP Central Station
records.short_description: Central control, data-processing, communications, and power-distribution hub for the Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Experiments Package.

details.overview: The ALSEP Central Station was the communications, command, data-handling, and power-distribution hub for the Apollo 12 lunar surface experiments. Instruments deployed around it sent measurements through the central station to Earth.
details.primary_purpose: Control the ALSEP experiments and collect, process, and transmit scientific and engineering data to the Manned Space Flight Network.
details.mission_role: It linked the Apollo 12 surface experiment instruments with ground controllers and distributed electrical power to the experiment package.

its_story.development: The central station was designed as the hub of the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package, allowing several experiments to continue after the astronauts returned to Earth.
its_story.preparation: It was carried to the lunar surface as part of the Apollo 12 ALSEP equipment and assembled at the selected deployment site.
its_story.journey: The central station travelled aboard the Apollo 12 Lunar Module Intrepid.
its_story.deployment: The Apollo 12 ALSEP was deployed on 1969-11-19. NASA records list the central station as first commanded on at 14:21 UT that day.
its_story.final_chapter: The Apollo 12 station was commanded off on 1977-09-30 when NASA terminated ALSEP support operations and data receipt.

why_is_it_there.scientific_engineering_need: The individual surface experiments needed a common system for power distribution, command reception, data collection, processing, and radio transmission.
why_is_it_there.mission_requirement: Apollo 12 included deployment of an ALSEP station to continue lunar geophysical and environmental measurements after the crew departed.
why_is_it_there.expected_purpose: Provide the central control and communications node for the Apollo 12 ALSEP array.
why_is_it_there.historical_context: The Apollo 12 array was the first full ALSEP deployed on the Moon and established a long-duration robotic science station.

how_was_it_built.design_and_construction: The central station combined the antenna and radio-frequency communications link with command, timing, data-processing, and power-distribution electronics. NASA-RP-1036 identifies the antenna as a modified axial-helical type, 58 cm long and 3.8 cm in diameter.
how_was_it_built.engineering_approach: The data subsystem used two separate transmitters, either selectable by command, with redundant sections in portions of the downlink configuration. The central station received commands, processed experiment and engineering data, and relayed formatted telemetry to Earth.
how_was_it_built.how_it_worked: The antenna received Earth-to-Moon commands and radiated Moon-to-Earth telemetry. The data subsystem conditioned, formatted, and routed scientific and engineering data to the selected transmitter; the power distribution system supplied the experiment and support subsystems.
how_was_it_built.power_source: The Apollo 12 ALSEP used a SNAP-27 radioisotope thermoelectric generator; the central station distributed power to the experiment system.
how_was_it_built.mobility_system: Stationary lunar-surface installation; deployed and aligned by the Apollo 12 crew.

contributions.explanation: The central station enabled several separately deployed experiments to be controlled and their data relayed to Earth after the crew left the Moon.
contributions.significance: It provided a reusable architecture for continuous, remotely managed lunar geophysical observations.

records.name: SNAP-27 Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator
records.short_description: Plutonium-238-powered radioisotope thermoelectric generator that supplied electrical power to the Apollo 12 ALSEP.

details.overview: The SNAP-27 Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator supplied electrical power to the Apollo 12 ALSEP, allowing its scientific instruments to operate on the lunar surface after the crew departed.
details.primary_purpose: Provide a long-duration electrical power source for the Apollo 12 lunar surface experiment package.
details.mission_role: Convert heat from plutonium-238 radioactive decay into electrical power for the ALSEP station and its instruments.

its_story.development: SNAP-27 was part of the Systems for Nuclear Auxiliary Power program and was developed as a radioisotope power source for Apollo lunar surface experiments.
its_story.preparation: The generator and its fuel element were transported as ALSEP hardware for deployment by the Apollo 12 crew.
its_story.journey: The SNAP-27 unit travelled to the Moon with the Apollo 12 ALSEP equipment.
its_story.deployment: It was deployed with the Apollo 12 ALSEP on 1969-11-19.
its_story.final_chapter: NASA reports that SNAP-27 units across the Apollo ALSEP missions operated for five to eight years until station shutdown in 1977. The reviewed sources do not establish the separate physical condition or exact final output of the Apollo 12 unit.

why_is_it_there.scientific_engineering_need: Long-duration lunar experiments required electrical power beyond the short period when astronauts were present and independent of direct sunlight.
why_is_it_there.mission_requirement: The ALSEP needed a power source capable of supporting unattended surface science through repeated lunar day and night cycles.
why_is_it_there.expected_purpose: Supply steady electrical power to the Apollo 12 ALSEP from radioisotope heat.
why_is_it_there.historical_context: Apollo 12 marked the first use of a nuclear power system on the lunar surface, according to NASA mission-history material.

how_was_it_built.design_and_construction: SNAP-27 was a plutonium-238 radioisotope thermoelectric generator. NASA-RP-1036 describes the generator assembly with its fuel capsule in place as 17 kg and identifies lead-telluride thermoelectric elements that converted decay heat into electrical power.
how_was_it_built.engineering_approach: Thermal energy from plutonium-238 decay was transferred to the generator's hot frame. Thermoelectric elements converted part of that heat directly into electrical power, while radiating fins rejected waste heat.
how_was_it_built.how_it_worked: The generator produced approximately 70 W DC at a nominal 16 V. Radioisotope decay supplied the thermal energy for thermoelectric conversion. The exact electrical output of the individual Apollo 12 unit after ALSEP termination is not established.
how_was_it_built.power_source: Plutonium-238 radioisotope heat source; this is the generator’s energy source, not an external electrical supply.
how_was_it_built.mobility_system: Stationary installation as part of the Apollo 12 ALSEP deployment.

records.name: Lunar Surface Magnetometer
records.short_description: The Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Magnetometer measured the Moon's surface magnetic field using three orthogonal sensors. NASA reports give both a preliminary 36 ± 5 gamma result and a later 38 ± 3 nT permanent-field value. It was permanently commanded OFF in 1974; later diagnostic checks did not restore valid data.

details.overview: The Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Magnetometer (LSM) was an ALSEP instrument that measured the magnetic field at the lunar surface. Its observations were used to study local lunar magnetism, solar-wind interactions, and electrical properties of the lunar interior.
details.primary_purpose: Measure the lunar-surface magnetic field and use the measurements to investigate the Moon’s electromagnetic properties and interior electrical characteristics.
details.mission_role: Provide stationary, continuous magnetic-field observations from the Apollo 12 landing site as part of the ALSEP science network.

its_story.development: The magnetometer extended magnetic-field measurement techniques to the lunar surface to study the Moon’s field and its interaction with solar and terrestrial magnetic environments.
its_story.preparation: The instrument was integrated into the Apollo 12 ALSEP array and carried to the lunar surface with the experiment package.
its_story.journey: It travelled to the Moon aboard the Apollo 12 Lunar Module Intrepid as part of ALSEP.
its_story.deployment: Conrad and Bean deployed the magnetometer on 1969-11-19. NASA-SP-235 Table 4-IV records 14:01 GMT, while its narrative passage states 14:00 G.m.t.; the report does not explain this one-minute variation. The instrument was turned ON at 14:39 GMT.
its_story.final_chapter: NASA’s ALSEP Termination Report states that the instrument was permanently commanded off on 1974-06-14 after its science and engineering data had remained static and invalid for approximately two years.

why_is_it_there.scientific_engineering_need: Surface magnetic measurements provide information about remanent lunar magnetism and the Moon’s response to changing external magnetic fields.
why_is_it_there.mission_requirement: The Apollo 12 objectives included deployment of the Lunar Surface Magnetometer as an ALSEP experiment.
why_is_it_there.expected_purpose: Measure lunar surface magnetic fields and infer aspects of the Moon’s deep-interior electrical properties.
why_is_it_there.historical_context: The Apollo 12 LSM produced the first in-situ measurement of an intrinsic lunar magnetic field, according to NASA’s later ALSEP science summary.

how_was_it_built.design_and_construction: The Apollo 12 magnetometer used three mutually orthogonal sensors at the ends of 100 cm booms. NASA-SP-235 states that the sensors were spread approximately 150 cm apart and were approximately 70 cm above the lunar surface. The report lists an instrument mass of 8.9 kg and dimensions of 25 × 28 × 63 cm.
how_was_it_built.engineering_approach: The three orthogonal fluxgate sensors measured vector magnetic-field components. NASA-SP-235 documents the 100 cm booms, approximately 150 cm sensor spread, and approximately 70 cm sensor height above the lunar surface, as well as the instrument's measurement and calibration functions.
how_was_it_built.how_it_worked: The instrument measured the three orthogonal components of the local magnetic field. The resulting time-series data supported analysis of the permanent local field and the Moon's response to changing external magnetic fields.
how_was_it_built.power_source: ALSEP central station power distribution, supplied by the SNAP-27 radioisotope thermoelectric generator.
how_was_it_built.mobility_system: Stationary surface instrument; deployed and oriented by the Apollo 12 crew.

discoveries.title: First in-situ measurement of an intrinsic lunar magnetic field
discoveries.explanation: The Apollo 12 LSM measured a permanent local magnetic field of approximately 38 ± 3 nT at the site. NASA’s termination report identifies this as the first in-situ measurement of an intrinsic lunar magnetic field.
discoveries.significance: The observation established that the Moon has localized remanent magnetic fields even though it lacks a strong global dipole field.

contributions.title: Lunar electromagnetic sounding
contributions.explanation: The LSM measurements, together with solar-wind observations and other magnetic measurements, were used to investigate electromagnetic excitation and estimate electrical conductivity within the Moon.
contributions.significance: The data contributed to early geophysical models of the lunar interior and its interaction with the solar wind.

records.name: Active Seismic Experiment
records.short_description: The Apollo 14 Active Seismic Experiment contributed seismic-refraction measurements of the lunar near-surface. NASA records that Apollo 14 central-station command capability was lost on 1975-03-05 and that the ASE status did not change at ALSEP termination on 1977-09-30. The equipment is classified INACTIVE from 1975-03-05; its last-contact date and physical condition remain UNKNOWN.

details.overview: The Apollo 14 Active Seismic Experiment (ASE) was a lunar-surface geophysical experiment designed to generate and monitor seismic waves. Its measurements were used to investigate the structure and physical properties of material beneath the Fra Mauro landing site.
details.primary_purpose: Study the physical structure of the lunar near-surface by measuring seismic-wave travel through subsurface layers.
details.mission_role: Provide active seismic measurements at the Fra Mauro landing site, complementing the passive seismic experiment and the wider Apollo seismic network.

its_story.development: The ASE was developed to obtain controlled seismic measurements rather than relying only on naturally occurring moonquakes or impacts.
its_story.preparation: The experiment was carried as part of the Apollo 14 ALSEP array. Its seismic sensors were deployed in the Fra Mauro area and connected to the ALSEP system; the reviewed NASA sources used for this record do not establish a verified exact geophone count.
its_story.journey: The equipment travelled to the Moon aboard the Apollo 14 Lunar Module Antares.
its_story.deployment: The experiment was deployed as part of the Apollo 14 ALSEP array during the first lunar-surface EVA on 1971-02-05.
its_story.final_chapter: NASA’s status table reports that the Apollo 14 ALSEP station failed during January 1976. The available sources reviewed do not establish an independent last-contact date or a separate physical failure state for the ASE instrument itself.

why_is_it_there.scientific_engineering_need: Seismic-wave measurements provide evidence about the thickness, layering, and physical properties of material beneath the lunar surface.
why_is_it_there.mission_requirement: Apollo 14 included an active seismic experiment to complement passive seismic observations and investigate the near-surface structure at Fra Mauro.
why_is_it_there.expected_purpose: Generate and monitor seismic waves to study the lunar subsurface to the depth range specified in the mission science plan.
why_is_it_there.historical_context: The experiment was the first active seismic package deployed on the lunar surface in the Apollo lunar-landing program.

how_was_it_built.design_and_construction: The ASE was an ALSEP geophysical instrument package. The high-level NASA sources used for this record do not establish a complete component-level bill of materials.
how_was_it_built.engineering_approach: The experiment generated seismic signals and recorded their propagation through the lunar near-surface so that wave behaviour could be used to infer subsurface layering. Hazardous source-operation details are intentionally not reproduced.
how_was_it_built.how_it_worked: The experiment generated and recorded seismic waves at the Fra Mauro site. The reviewed high-level NASA sources support its scientific purpose and results but do not provide a complete electronics-level or component-level description.
how_was_it_built.power_source: ALSEP central station electrical power, supplied by the station power system.
how_was_it_built.mobility_system: Stationary lunar-surface deployment. Seismic sensors were positioned in the ALSEP deployment area and connected to the central station; no exact geophone count is asserted in this record.

discoveries.title: Evidence for an approximately 8.5 m regolith layer at Fra Mauro
discoveries.explanation: The initial ASE seismic interpretation indicated an approximately 8.5 m thick surficial layer with a P-wave velocity of 104 m/s. NASA interpreted this layer as regolith.
discoveries.significance: The measurements provided a direct seismic constraint on the thickness and physical properties of the upper lunar surface material at the Apollo 14 site.

contributions.title: Active seismic characterization of the lunar near-surface
contributions.explanation: The ASE supplied seismic-refraction measurements at Fra Mauro, complementing the Apollo passive seismic network and supporting interpretation of subsurface layers.
contributions.significance: It expanded Apollo lunar geophysics from passive event detection to controlled near-surface seismic investigation.

records.name: Charged Particle Lunar Environment Experiment
records.short_description: Apollo 14 ALSEP charged-particle instrument that measured low-energy electron and ion fluxes from the lunar surface environment.

details.overview: The Charged Particle Lunar Environment Experiment (CPLEE) was an Apollo 14 ALSEP instrument designed to measure low-energy charged particles reaching the lunar surface. Its two analyzers observed particles in two viewing directions and provided measurements of the lunar plasma environment, including solar-wind and Earth-magnetotail conditions.
details.primary_purpose: Measure energy spectra and fluxes of low-energy electrons and ions at the lunar surface, helping characterize the solar wind, magnetotail plasma, photoelectrons and lunar surface electrical environment.
details.mission_role: Provided in-situ charged-particle measurements at the Fra Mauro ALSEP station, complementing other Apollo plasma and geophysical experiments.

its_story.development: Developed as a charged-particle experiment for Apollo 14 to investigate the plasma environment at the lunar surface. NASA SP-272 identifies the instrument as a pair of ion-electron spectrometers.
its_story.preparation: The instrument was part of the Apollo 14 ALSEP package and was connected to the ALSEP central station. Its apertures were protected by a dust cover during deployment and lunar-module ascent.
its_story.journey: Carried to the Moon aboard the Apollo 14 Lunar Module as part of the ALSEP equipment.
its_story.deployment: Deployed northeast of the ALSEP central station at Fra Mauro at approximately 18:00 GMT on 1971-02-05. NASA reports that it was leveled and aligned using a bubble level and Sun compass.
its_story.final_chapter: After several years of operation and periods of standby associated with instrument and station conditions, CPLEE was configured to STANDBY at the end of ALSEP termination testing on 1977-09-30.

why_is_it_there.scientific_engineering_need: The Moon provides a surface environment with little atmosphere and a weak global magnetic field, allowing charged particles and plasma conditions to be measured without the strong atmospheric and magnetic effects found at Earth.
why_is_it_there.mission_requirement: Apollo 14 included an ALSEP instrument package for long-duration, automated geophysical and space-environment measurements after the crew departed.
why_is_it_there.expected_purpose: Measure low-energy charged-particle fluxes and their energy distributions, including solar-wind and magnetotail populations and photoelectrons emitted from the sunlit lunar surface.
why_is_it_there.historical_context: CPLEE contributed to the Apollo network of lunar surface experiments by measuring plasma phenomena at a second widely separated lunar site.

how_was_it_built.design_and_construction: A box-shaped instrument supported by four legs. NASA SP-272 describes two physical charged-particle analyzers and associated data-handling electronics.
how_was_it_built.engineering_approach: Two analyzers observed particles in different directions, enabling comparison of charged-particle fluxes and energy distributions at the lunar surface.
how_was_it_built.how_it_worked: The analyzers measured the energy distributions and fluxes of incoming electrons and ions. Data and housekeeping information were sent through the ALSEP central station for transmission to Earth.
how_was_it_built.power_source: ALSEP central-station electrical supply. NASA SP-272 reports approximately 3.0 W normal power dissipation and approximately 6.0 W with the lunar-night survival heater operating. NASA-RP-1036 separately lists 6.5 W total power. These are source-specific report values and are retained without selecting one as universally applicable.
scientific_instruments: Two physical charged-particle analyzers for electron and ion measurements

discoveries.title: Lunar surface photoelectron and electrical-potential observations
discoveries.explanation: CPLEE measurements showed that the sunlit lunar surface produced a photoelectron population. NASA RP-1036 reports that the surface reached a positive potential of about 200 V under low-density plasma conditions.
discoveries.significance: The observations helped characterize the electrical state of the lunar surface and the interaction between solar radiation, charged particles and lunar material.

contributions.explanation: CPLEE provided direct measurements of low-energy charged particles at the Apollo 14 site, complementing measurements from other Apollo ALSEP stations.

records.name: Heat Flow Experiment
records.short_description: Apollo 15 ALSEP experiment that measured temperature and thermal properties in the lunar subsurface to determine heat flow from the Moon’s interior.

details.overview: The Apollo 15 Heat Flow Experiment (HFE) measured temperature variations and thermal properties in the lunar subsurface to determine how heat escapes from the Moon’s interior. Two probes were emplaced in the regolith at Hadley Rille and connected by cables to an electronics package and the ALSEP station.
details.primary_purpose: Determine the rate of heat flow from the lunar interior by measuring subsurface temperature gradients and thermal conductivity.
details.mission_role: Provided direct subsurface thermal measurements at the Hadley Rille Apollo 15 site, complementing lunar surface temperature measurements and returned sample studies.

its_story.development: The HFE was developed to make direct measurements of lunar subsurface temperatures and thermal conductivity rather than relying only on remote observations.
its_story.preparation: The Apollo 15 instrument used two probes, connecting cables and an electronics unit. The probes were installed in holes prepared in the lunar regolith.
its_story.journey: Carried to the Moon as part of the Apollo 15 ALSEP science package.
its_story.deployment: The Apollo 15 HFE was deployed at Hadley Rille on 1971-07-31. NASA SP-289 reports borestem penetration of 1.62 m at Probe 1 and approximately 1.60 m at Probe 2. The probe itself was inserted approximately 1.40 m into Probe 1 borestem (Figure 11-3); Probe 2 insertion was obstructed near 1.0 m. The later NASA NTRS restoration abstract separately reports approximate probe penetration depths of 1.4 m and 1.0 m. NASA SP-289 reports the two probe locations approximately 10 m apart, while the later restoration abstract reports roughly 8.5 m; both source-specific separation values are preserved. Although the obstruction prevented valid ring- and gradient-bridge measurements from Probe 2 upper section during most of the lunation cycle, the lower sensors still provided useful subsurface temperature data.
its_story.final_chapter: NASA NTRS describes HFE operation from July 1971 through January 1977. NASA-RP-1036 documents intermittent operation from 1976-04-28 and anomalous data since December 1975, followed by a commanded OFF on 1977-01-15. The earlier and later heat-flow results remain identified by their respective report stages.

why_is_it_there.scientific_engineering_need: Measurements of heat escaping from the lunar interior help constrain the Moon’s internal temperature, thermal evolution and abundance of heat-producing radioactive elements.
why_is_it_there.mission_requirement: Apollo 15 included long-duration ALSEP measurements that could continue after the astronauts left the surface.
why_is_it_there.expected_purpose: Measure subsurface temperature gradients and thermal conductivity at Hadley Rille to estimate local lunar heat flow.
why_is_it_there.historical_context: The Apollo 15 and Apollo 17 heat-flow experiments provided the successful lunar heat-flow measurements from the Apollo program; the Apollo 16 unit did not provide useful measurements because of a cable problem, a distinction documented in NASA sources.

how_was_it_built.design_and_construction: The Apollo 15 HFE used two subsurface probes connected by approximately 8 m cables to an electronics box, which connected to the ALSEP station. Each probe carried multiple temperature sensors.
how_was_it_built.engineering_approach: Temperature sensors measured temperature at several depths and along the cable, while heater-based measurements provided thermal-conductivity information. These data were used to calculate the heat flow from the lunar interior.
how_was_it_built.how_it_worked: The probes recorded temperatures at multiple depths. Changes in temperature with depth and controlled thermal measurements were used to estimate thermal conductivity and the heat flow through the lunar subsurface.
how_was_it_built.power_source: ALSEP central-station electrical supply; NASA-RP-1036 lists 9.0 W total power for the Heat Flow Experiment.
scientific_instruments: Gradient bridges: one per probe section; measure temperature differences between sensors separated by 47 cm.
Ring bridges: one per probe section; measure temperature differences between sensors separated by 28 cm.
Cable thermocouples: four per probe, spaced along the first 2.5 m of cable above the probe.
Thermocouple reference bridge: one per experiment, mounted on the electronics-box radiation plate.

records.name: Lunar Surface Magnetometer
records.short_description: Apollo 15 ALSEP triaxial fluxgate magnetometer that measured the lunar surface magnetic field and its response to solar and terrestrial magnetic fields.

details.overview: The Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Magnetometer (LSM) was a three-axis instrument deployed at Hadley Rille. It measured the lunar surface magnetic field and its variations, contributing to investigations of remanent lunar magnetism, the Moon’s electrical properties and its interaction with the solar wind.
details.primary_purpose: Measure three orthogonal components of the magnetic field at the Apollo 15 site and help investigate the Moon’s internal electrical properties and response to external magnetic fields.
details.mission_role: Provided one station in the Apollo lunar-surface magnetometer network and supplied magnetic-field measurements that could be compared with other ALSEP and solar-wind observations.

its_story.development: The Apollo 15 LSM was part of a network of lunar surface magnetometers intended to measure remanent magnetic fields and the Moon’s response to large-scale solar and terrestrial magnetic fields.
its_story.preparation: The instrument used three fluxgate sensors mounted at the ends of three orthogonal 100 cm booms, with electronics housed in a thermally insulated package.
its_story.journey: Carried to the Moon as part of the Apollo 15 ALSEP science package.
its_story.deployment: NASA SP-289 records deployment at 18:29 GMT on 1971-07-31 at 26°26′ N, 3°29′ E in the Hadley Rille region.
its_story.final_chapter: The Apollo 15 instrument developed sensor and data anomalies. NASA-RP-1036 records a permanent OFF command on 1974-06-14; later inadvertent ON commands in 1975 were followed by OFF commands and did not restore valid science data.

why_is_it_there.scientific_engineering_need: Magnetic-field measurements can reveal remanent magnetization in lunar materials and help constrain the Moon’s electrical conductivity and internal structure.
why_is_it_there.mission_requirement: Apollo 15 extended the lunar surface geophysical network with a magnetometer station at Hadley Rille.
why_is_it_there.expected_purpose: Continuously measure and transmit the lunar magnetic field over a planned one-year operating period.
why_is_it_there.historical_context: The Apollo 15 measurements complemented the Apollo 12 and Apollo 14 magnetometer investigations and enabled comparison of local magnetic fields across widely separated lunar sites.

how_was_it_built.design_and_construction: A triaxial fluxgate magnetometer with three orthogonal sensors mounted at the ends of 100 cm booms. The electronics were housed in a thermally insulated package.
how_was_it_built.engineering_approach: Each sensor measured one orthogonal component of the magnetic-field vector. Internal calibration and sensor-flip sequences were used to monitor offsets and instrument performance.
how_was_it_built.how_it_worked: The fluxgate sensors measured the three vector components of the local magnetic field. Electronics processed the measurements and sent the data through the ALSEP central-station radio link to Earth.
how_was_it_built.power_source: ALSEP central-station electrical supply; NASA SP-289 lists average power of 3.5 W during lunar day and 9.4 W during lunar night.

discoveries.title: Local remanent magnetic field at Hadley Rille
discoveries.explanation: NASA SP-289 reports a remanent magnetic field of 6 ± 4 gamma at the Apollo 15 site. The report compares this with stronger values measured at Apollo 12 and Apollo 14 and concludes that the observed remanent field strengths vary substantially from site to site.
discoveries.significance: The site-to-site differences supported the interpretation that the measured remanent magnetic sources were local rather than a single global lunar field.

contributions.explanation: The LSM data contributed to studies of lunar electrical conductivity, internal structure and magnetic-field interactions with the solar wind.
contributions.significance: The instrument provided a long-duration surface magnetic record that could be analyzed alongside solar-wind measurements and data from other lunar stations.

records.name: Apollo 15 Solar Wind Spectrometer
records.short_description: Apollo 15 ALSEP spectrometer that measured the direction and energy of solar-wind electrons and positive ions reaching the lunar surface.

details.overview: The Apollo 15 Solar Wind Spectrometer (SWS) measured the direction and energy of charged particles in the solar wind and magnetotail plasma reaching the lunar surface. Its seven Faraday-cup sensors provided directional measurements over much of the sky above the lunar horizon.
details.primary_purpose: Measure the energy and direction of solar-wind electrons and positive ions at the lunar surface and study their interaction with local magnetic fields and the lunar photoelectron layer.
details.mission_role: Provided in-situ solar-plasma measurements at Hadley Rille and enabled comparison with the Apollo 12 solar-wind spectrometer data from a second lunar site.

its_story.development: The Apollo 15 SWS was designed to measure solar-wind plasma at the lunar surface and compare the measurements with data from the Apollo 12 site and near-lunar space.
its_story.preparation: The instrument used seven Faraday-cup sensors arranged to measure particle flux from different directions. Its sensor openings remained covered during deployment and Lunar Module ascent.
its_story.journey: Carried to the Moon as part of the Apollo 15 ALSEP package.
its_story.deployment: The SWS was deployed near the end of the first Apollo 15 EVA on 1971-07-31. It was first turned on for background measurements with sensor covers in place; the covers were removed by command on 1971-08-02 after Lunar Module ascent.
its_story.final_chapter: NASA-RP-1036 records static and invalid science/engineering data from 1972-06-30, followed by a permanent OFF command on 1974-06-14. Diagnostic ON checks followed on 1974-07-03, 1974-07-29 and 1974-09-03, but no valid science or engineering data were returned. Spurious command events in 1975 and 1976 occurred later and are documented separately; they did not restore useful science operation.

why_is_it_there.scientific_engineering_need: The solar wind is a stream of charged particles from the Sun. Measuring it at the lunar surface helps characterize plasma conditions and how the solar wind interacts with the Moon and local magnetic fields.
why_is_it_there.mission_requirement: Apollo 15 expanded the ALSEP plasma-observation capability and enabled simultaneous comparison with the Apollo 12 SWS at a distant lunar site.
why_is_it_there.expected_purpose: Measure electron and positive-ion fluxes, particle energies and arrival directions; investigate the lunar photoelectric layer and possible plasma changes near lunar dawn and dusk.
why_is_it_there.historical_context: The Apollo 15 SWS became one of two lunar-surface solar-wind spectrometers described in the Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report.

how_was_it_built.design_and_construction: A surface spectrometer with seven modulated Faraday-cup sensors. The sensor cups were arranged to cover much of the upward hemisphere, while the electronics package was housed in a temperature-controlled container below the sensor assembly.
how_was_it_built.engineering_approach: Each Faraday cup measured charged-particle flux. The instrument measured particle energies in sequential energy steps and compared the relative responses among cups to estimate particle direction and anisotropy.
how_was_it_built.how_it_worked: The seven cups measured incoming charged-particle fluxes from different directions. Sequential energy measurements provided information about electron and positive-ion energy distributions and the direction of plasma flow.
how_was_it_built.power_source: ALSEP central-station electrical supply; NASA-RP-1036 lists total SWS power as 12.5 W.

discoveries.title: Apollo 15 solar-wind and electron observations
discoveries.explanation: NASA-RP-1036 reports an approximately 3-gamma local magnetic field at the Apollo 15 site. Proton measurements showed no measurable difference from upstream solar-wind data. Electron observations were broadly similar to expected upstream values, with occasional directional particle shadowing and lunar photoelectrons in the lowest-energy channels.
discoveries.significance: These observations characterized how the solar-wind plasma and low-energy electron population were measured at the Apollo 15 lunar surface site.

discoveries.title: Contrasting solar-wind observations at Apollo 12 and Apollo 15
discoveries.explanation: The 1975 comparison paper reports stronger solar-wind perturbations at Apollo 12 than at Apollo 15. The Apollo 12 site had a relatively stronger local magnetic field; Apollo 15 observations showed no noticeable differences from upstream solar-wind properties.
discoveries.significance: The two-site comparison provided evidence that local lunar environments differed in their observed interaction with the solar wind.

contributions.title: Simultaneous lunar-surface plasma observations
contributions.explanation: The Apollo 15 SWS joined the Apollo 12 SWS as a second solar-wind spectrometer on the lunar surface. NASA SP-289 notes that the two instruments were separated by approximately 1,100 km and offered the opportunity to compare solar plasma at two locations.
contributions.significance: The two-site measurements supported comparisons of solar-wind plasma conditions and their interaction with the Moon.

contributions.title: Comparative observations of the solar wind at two lunar sites
contributions.explanation: The Apollo 12/Apollo 15 study compared spectrometer observations from two lunar locations and reported stronger solar-wind perturbations at Apollo 12 than at Apollo 15, alongside the difference in their local magnetic-field environments.
contributions.significance: The comparison helped investigate how local lunar magnetic environments relate to solar-wind plasma observations at the lunar surface.

mission_timeline.title: Solar Wind Spectrometer deployed
mission_timeline.description: The SWS was deployed near the end of the first Apollo 15 EVA.

mission_timeline.title: Background measurements began
mission_timeline.description: The SWS was turned on at 19:37:10 GMT with its sensor covers still in place to provide background data.

mission_timeline.title: Sensor covers removed and solar-plasma detection began
mission_timeline.description: At 18:07:32 GMT, approximately one hour after Lunar Module ascent, the sensor covers were removed by command from Earth and detection of solar plasma began.

mission_timeline.title: Intermittent proton-energy modulation drops
mission_timeline.description: NASA-RP-1036 reports intermittent modulation drops in proton energy levels 13 and 14 for the Apollo 12 and Apollo 15 SWS. The thermally induced problem occurred each lunation and was attributed to a circuit used solely for ground-test purposes.

mission_timeline.title: Science and engineering data became static and invalid
mission_timeline.description: NASA-RP-1036 reports that high-voltage arcing in the SWS electronics caused excessive power consumption. Because the additional load could not be tolerated by the Apollo 15 ALSEP system, the instrument was left in STANDBY indefinitely. OPERATE SELECT commands were periodically issued to check for any change in instrument status.

mission_timeline.title: Permanent OFF command
mission_timeline.description: NASA-RP-1036 records the Apollo 15 SWS permanently commanded OFF on 1974-06-14 after data had been static and invalid since 1972-06-30.

mission_timeline.title: Post-shutdown diagnostic ON check
mission_timeline.description: NASA-RP-1036 lists a diagnostic ON check during real-time support; no valid scientific or engineering data were received.

mission_timeline.title: Post-shutdown diagnostic ON check
mission_timeline.description: NASA-RP-1036 lists a diagnostic ON check; no valid scientific or engineering data were received. The reserve-power change was 6.00 W.

mission_timeline.title: Post-shutdown diagnostic ON check
mission_timeline.description: NASA-RP-1036 records both Apollo 12 and Apollo 15 instruments commanded ON; power draw was negligible and no valid scientific or engineering data were returned.

mission_timeline.title: Inadvertent ON command followed by OFF
mission_timeline.description: NASA-RP-1036 records a spurious functional ON command on 1975-01-25, causing a 3.9 W reserve-power drain. The instrument was commanded to STANDBY, with no reserve-power change, and then to OFF; reserve power increased by 3.9 W.

mission_timeline.title: Inadvertent standby-power command followed by OFF
mission_timeline.description: NASA-RP-1036 records a spurious STANDBY POWER ON command on 1975-09-15, causing a 4 W reserve-power drain attributed to the standby heater turning on. The instrument was commanded OFF, after which reserve power increased by 4 W.

mission_timeline.title: Spurious ON command followed by OFF
mission_timeline.description: NASA-RP-1036 records a spurious functional ON command on 1976-01-31. The Guam Tracking Station commanded the experiment OFF; no increase or decrease in reserve power was observed.

mission_timeline.title: ALSEP program termination — no change in SWS status
mission_timeline.description: NASA-RP-1036 records no change in Solar-Wind Spectrometer status when the ALSEP program was terminated. The entry applies to Apollo 12 and Apollo 15; it does not record a new OFF command.

records.name: Active Seismic Experiment
records.short_description: Apollo 16 ALSEP instrument that used a three-geophone array to record seismic waves and investigate the shallow subsurface at the Descartes highlands landing site. Hazardous seismic-source subsystem details are intentionally omitted.

details.overview: The Apollo 16 Active Seismic Experiment (ASE) was a lunar-surface instrument within the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP). It used a three-geophone array and associated signal-processing electronics to record seismic waves and investigate the shallow subsurface at the Descartes highlands site. This research record documents the geophone system and scientific results only; it intentionally excludes construction, specifications and operation of hazardous seismic-source hardware.
details.primary_purpose: To generate and monitor seismic waves in order to estimate the thickness and seismic properties of the lunar near-surface materials and identify subsurface velocity boundaries at the Apollo 16 Descartes site.
details.mission_role: Provided a local active-seismic survey at the Apollo 16 highlands landing site, complementing the broader lunar seismic network and earlier Apollo landing-site measurements.

its_story.development: The ASE was developed as an Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP) experiment for local lunar seismology. NASA's Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report documents the experiment's scientific purpose, receiving array and results. This record limits its technical description to the geophone measurement system.
its_story.preparation: The experiment was integrated into the Apollo 16 ALSEP surface-science package. This record documents only the receiving and measurement system and does not describe hazardous source hardware or its preparation.
its_story.journey: The ASE was carried to the Moon as part of the Apollo 16 lunar surface experiment payload and deployed at the Descartes highlands site.
its_story.deployment: The Apollo 16 ASE's three-geophone receiving array was deployed at the Descartes highlands ALSEP site during lunar surface operations. NASA's report describes the array as aligned at a bearing of 287 degrees clockwise from north relative to the ALSEP central station. NASA's ALSEP status table separately records the Apollo 16 array commanded ON at 19:38 GMT on 1972-04-21; that array-level command time is not assigned to the geophone deployment. The precise individual geophone coordinates and the exact deployment time are UNKNOWN in the sources used here.
its_story.final_chapter: NASA records the Apollo 16 ALSEP array commanded OFF on 1977-09-30, when ALSEP support operations ended. This supports program-level decommissioning of the ASE. The current physical condition of the individual geophones and other components is UNKNOWN.

why_is_it_there.scientific_engineering_need: Remote observations cannot directly provide the same local seismic measurements of lunar surface materials. The ASE was intended to use recorded seismic waves to investigate near-surface structure at the Apollo 16 site.
why_is_it_there.mission_requirement: Apollo 16's highlands landing site provided an opportunity to add an active-seismic profile from a geological setting distinct from the earlier Apollo landing sites.
why_is_it_there.expected_purpose: Measure seismic-wave travel behaviour across a geophone array to estimate near-surface seismic velocities and identify subsurface boundaries.
why_is_it_there.historical_context: The experiment extended the Apollo lunar seismic investigation to the Descartes highlands. The record keeps Apollo 16 results distinct from Apollo 14 results.

how_was_it_built.design_and_construction: The documented receiving portion of the Apollo 16 ASE consisted of three geophones, their interconnecting cable, and the associated experiment electronics. Details of the experiment's hazardous seismic-source hardware are intentionally excluded.
how_was_it_built.engineering_approach: A three-geophone receiving array detected ground motion from seismic waves. The received signals were amplified, compressed, digitized and transmitted through the ALSEP telemetry system for scientific analysis.
key_components: ALSEP experiment electronics and telemetry interface
how_was_it_built.how_it_worked: Seismic waves reaching the lunar surface caused ground motion detected by the geophones. Their signals passed through the receiving electronics for conditioning, digital recording and transmission to Earth. This description is limited to the receiving and measurement chain.
how_was_it_built.mobility_system: Stationary surface instrument after deployment; no self-propelled mobility system.
scientific_instruments: Three miniature moving-coil/magnet geophones arranged as a linear receiving array.

discoveries.title: Two-layer near-surface seismic velocity structure at the Apollo 16 Descartes site
discoveries.explanation: Apollo 16 ASE preliminary analysis identified a 114 m/s compressional-wave velocity in the surface layer, interpreted as lunar regolith. A faster 250 m/s refracting horizon was estimated at 12.2 m depth. NASA treated the deeper material's geological identity as preliminary rather than definitively established.
discoveries.significance: The result provided an in-situ seismic constraint on the shallow highlands subsurface and helped distinguish the regolith from the underlying material at the Descartes landing site.

contributions.title: Apollo 16 highlands active-seismic profile
contributions.explanation: The ASE added an active-seismic profile from the Descartes highlands, providing a measured near-surface velocity and evidence for a deeper, faster refracting horizon. NASA compared the 114 m/s Apollo 16 surface-layer result with earlier Apollo landing-site values; those earlier values are comparisons only, not Apollo 16 measurements.
contributions.significance: The experiment expanded the geographic coverage of lunar near-surface seismic measurements into a highlands setting and supported comparative studies of lunar regolith properties.

mission_timeline.title: Apollo 16 lunar landing
mission_timeline.description: The Apollo 16 lunar module landed in the Descartes region. The lunar landing established the site for deployment of the ALSEP science package, including the ASE.

mission_timeline.description: NASA's ALSEP status table records the Apollo 16 array commanded ON at 19:38 GMT. This is an array-level command timestamp; it is not the geophone-array deployment time. mission_timeline.title: Apollo 16 ALSEP operations terminated
mission_timeline.description: NASA's ALSEP status table records the Apollo 16 array commanded OFF on 1977-09-30. NASA's ALSEP history identifies this as the program-wide decommissioning date. The milestone does not establish the present physical condition of individual ASE components.

mission_timeline.title: Apollo 16 returned to Earth
mission_timeline.description: The Apollo 16 mission returned to Earth. This closes the crewed mission chronology; it does not mark the end of the surface ASE's automated operation, which continued as part of ALSEP until 1977.

status.explanation: NASA's ALSEP status table records the Apollo 16 array commanded ON on 1972-04-21 at 19:38 GMT and commanded OFF on 1977-09-30. This supports DECOMMISSIONED as the experiment's program-level operational classification. It does not establish the present physical condition of individual ASE components, which remains UNKNOWN.

records.name: InSight Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package (HP³)
records.short_description: HP³ was InSight’s Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package. Its self-hammering mole was designed to penetrate several metres into the ground while a tether and sensors measured subsurface temperature and thermal properties.

details.overview: HP³ was InSight’s Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package. Its self-hammering mole was designed to penetrate several metres into the ground while a tether and sensors measured subsurface temperature and thermal properties.
details.primary_purpose: Measure heat escaping from Mars’ interior and characterize thermal properties of the shallow subsurface.
details.mission_role: Attempt a direct measurement of Martian heat flow using a self-hammering mole, a tether with temperature sensors and a radiometer.

its_story.final_chapter: The InSight mission ended in December 2022. This mission-level end does not mean the instrument was physically removed.

how_was_it_built.design_and_construction: HP³ included a self-hammering mole, a science tether carrying temperature sensors, heaters and thermal sensors, a radiometer, and support/electronics hardware. NASA Science reports mass about 3 kg including control electronics, maximum power 2 W while burrowing and total volume about 20 L. The mole reached only about 35 cm and did not achieve its planned 3–5 m depth.

contributions.title: Engineering lessons from HP³ subsurface penetration attempt
contributions.explanation: The HP³ mole encountered regolith behaviour that did not provide sufficient friction for its self-hammering mechanism to advance to the intended depth. The mission’s attempts to assist the mole generated operational and engineering experience for future planetary subsurface systems.
contributions.significance: The attempt documented the challenges of penetrating Martian regolith with a self-hammering probe; the intended deep heat-flow measurement was not achieved.
